notes:
I've arranged the notes verse by verse. A few things you should know first:

- **Some verses are thin.** My fetch of Enduring Word cut off partway through v. 15, and I couldn't read the full Precept Austin, Bible.org (Utley) or Bible Hub pages. Notes on vv. 16 and 21–25 come only from search snippets.
- **Missing sources.** I found nothing from the Methodist sites (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), the Orthodox site (oca.org), New Advent, or NET Bible notes on these verses.
- **No popular modern teaching.** I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage, so that category is left out.
- **Unnamed authors.** Where a page gathers several commentaries and the snippet didn't name the writer, I say so rather than guess.

---

**vv. 1–4 (the preface)**
- These four verses are one Greek sentence in a polished style. After them Luke switches to everyday language, because he wanted readers to understand Jesus, not admire Luke. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/
- Lenski (a Lutheran commentator, quoted on Precept Austin) says the sentence matches the best Greek historians. Norval Geldenhuys comments: "Luke here uses pragma instead of hrema, and in this way makes it clear that it is here not a question of mere narratives, but of actual historical facts." https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-1-commentary
- Modern scholarship: Luke's prologue is similar to other introductions found in ancient texts, and scholars generally classify these as belonging to the Greco-Roman genre of history. The same article finds in the Gospel as a whole a mix of solid historical data and imaginative reconstruction. That judgment is aimed mainly at the birth story in Luke 2. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/was-luke-a-historian/

**v. 1** – The "many" accounts may mean Mark and Matthew, and possibly other writings about Jesus that were not inspired. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/ Ligonier suggests several stories about Jesus were already circulating, probably accounts of single episodes, and Luke wanted to give a fuller history. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/witness-luke

**v. 2** – The eyewitnesses were the apostles, and also people like Mary, whom Luke probably interviewed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/ Piper says these were not ordinary witnesses: they were the apostles, carrying the authority of the risen Lord. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-aim-of-dr-luke Utley (Bible.org) notes that "handed down" is the Greek word often translated "traditions". "From the beginning" could mean either the birth events or the start of Jesus' ministry. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21296

**v. 3** – Luke was not an eyewitness, but he places himself alongside the eyewitness writers because his account rests on careful research. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/ MacArthur says the prologue promises an ordered account, but this does not mean he always followed a strict chronological order in all instances. He dates the Gospel to about AD 60–61. https://www.gty.org/library/bible-introductions/MSB42/Luke
- **Theophilus:**
  - The name means "lover of God". It may be a nickname, and "most excellent" may point to a well-known Roman official. https://www.gty.org/library/bible-introductions/MSB42/Luke
  - Utley lists three theories: a Roman official, a wealthy patron, or a coded name for some Christian. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21296
  - Guzik thinks Luke–Acts may have been Paul's defence brief for his trial before Caesar. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/
  - GotQuestions leans towards a high-ranking or influential Gentile. https://www.gotquestions.org/Theophilus-Luke-Acts.html

**v. 4** – Theophilus had already been taught the faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/ Ligonier frames the purpose as giving him certainty; Luke wrote under the Holy Spirit's inspiration. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/witness-luke

**v. 5** – "In the days of Herod" ties the story to a real time. This is Herod the Great, an Edomite near the end of a cruel reign. The priestly divisions, including Abijah's, are listed in 1 Chronicles 23–24. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/

**v. 6** – Precept Austin: the couple lived godly lives amid the almost universal corruption of the priesthood. "Blameless" describes the overall direction of their walk, not perfection. The page also stresses that Old Testament saints were saved through faith alone. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-1-commentary

**v. 7** – Their righteousness sat alongside the stigma of childlessness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/ Desiring God pairs this verse with v. 27: Zechariah's wife is barren and Mary is a virgin, so both are "equally unfit" to have a child. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/lukes-lesson-on-grace-and-faith

**vv. 8–10** – Guzik:
- There were perhaps 20,000 priests, so lots decided duties, and the incense lot was likely a once-in-a-lifetime honour.
- He describes the temple routine in detail: three lots, and the incense priest left alone before the curtain.
- Burning incense pictures prayer (Ps 141:2; Rev 5:8). Zechariah probably prayed for the nation and for the Messiah.

https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/

**vv. 11–12** – This angel was a glorious and frightening figure, not a winged baby, which is why he begins "Do not be afraid." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/ Precept Austin adds that the angel's appearance could have meant judgment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-1-commentary

**v. 13 – what prayer was heard? (commentators differ)**
- Ellicott: the prayer was not that he might have a son (that hope appears to have died out long before), but that the Kingdom of God might come. https://biblehub.com/luke/1-13.htm
- Guzik agrees he probably wasn't praying for a son, and says God answered both longings at once. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/
- A Precept Austin comment instead says, Yet he was praying for a son! https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-1-commentary
- The name John was a command from the Lord, given before he was even conceived. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/

**v. 14** – Ryle (Anglican) says no children bring such true joy as those who have God's grace. https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/articles/onsite/exposition113.html

**v. 15**
- **No wine:** this likely points to the Nazirite vow of Numbers 6. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/ The same reading appears in Everett's notes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/luke-1.html
- **Filled with the Spirit:** Calvin, quoted by Guzik, says "from the earliest infancy to the latest old age, the operation of the Spirit in men is free." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/
- MacArthur counts this as the first mark of John's true greatness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-1-commentary
- A Bible Hub article calls the filling vocational, equipping John as a prophet, rather than regenerative in the Pauline sense. It notes that Irenaeus and Augustine cited this verse. https://biblehub.com/q/Luke_1_15_Spirit-filled_from_birth.htm
- **Where traditions differ – infants and grace:**
  - *Anglican (Ryle):* children are never too young for grace, and If an infant can be filled with the Holy Spirit, he is surely not unworthy to be admitted into the visible church. https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/articles/onsite/exposition113.html
  - *Lutheran (1517):* using John's leap in v. 41, which fulfils v. 15, the writer answers the claim that babies can't believe: it was a leap of faith. https://www.1517.org/articles/baptism-now-saves-but-who-and-when
  - *Lutheran (LCMS Indiana District):* the unborn John met God's Word, through which the Spirit creates faith. https://in.lcms.org/a-leaping-baby-the-visitation/
  - *Baptist (Piper):* uses the verse for personhood, not baptism: Only *persons* are filled with the Spirit. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-baby-in-my-womb-leaped-for-joy
  - I found no Baptist source arguing directly against Ryle's infant-baptism point.

**v. 17** – Henry Morris (Precept Austin) says this verse paraphrases Malachi 4:6. John was not Elijah returned to earth; he came in Elijah's spirit and power. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-1-commentary "Before Him" refers to the Messiah. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-1-commentary

**v. 18 – how serious was Zechariah's doubt? (commentators differ)**
- *Strong view:*
  - Guzik: he wanted to believe but thought it too good to be true, and looked at circumstances before God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/
  - Sproul (Reformed) calls it the "egregious sin of unbelief," in effect saying God can't be trusted. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/angel-zacharias-part-3
  - Precept Austin says the Greek "not" in v. 20 expresses total unbelief. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-1-commentary
- *Milder view:*
  - An older commentary on Bible Hub (author not named in the snippet) says he asked a sign for the further increase and confirmation of his faith, and his punishment was gentle. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-19.htm
  - Constable thinks Gabriel went easy on him because he believed and only wanted confirmation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-19.html
- *Comparison with Mary:* Mary asked almost the same question, but out of faith; Zechariah asked out of skepticism. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/

**v. 19**
- Calvin: Gabriel shows that it was God's truthfulness, not the angel's, that had been doubted. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-19.html
- Gabriel appears only to Daniel, Zechariah and Mary. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/luke-1.html
- Commentators on Bible Hub (names not given in the snippet) offer several points:
  - The name means "man of God" or "power of God".
  - It reminded Zechariah of Daniel's prophecies about the Messiah.
  - Gabriel is the messenger of good news, as Michael is of judgment.

  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-19.htm
- "Bring you good news" is Gabriel "preaching the gospel" to Zechariah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/

**v. 20**
- Spurgeon: Zacharias had asked for a sign, and by a sign he was chastened. He adds that the Lord will not use an unbelieving messenger. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons-verse-exposition-luke
- Guzik: unbelief didn't cancel God's promise; it only kept Zechariah from enjoying it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/
- John Martin (Bible Knowledge Commentary): for nine months Zechariah's failed attempts to speak would prove the message true. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-1-commentary

**vv. 21–25**
- Everett treats these verses as the fulfilment of Gabriel's words: Zechariah is struck mute and Elizabeth conceives. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/luke-1.html
- Constable says the muteness also conceal[ed] Gabriel's revelation from the people until the proper time. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-19.html
- Precept Austin quotes a writer (not named in the snippet) noting that Zechariah, though struck dumb, kept up his work for the Lord. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-1-commentary

**v. 26**
- "In the sixth month" means the sixth month of Elizabeth's pregnancy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/
- Matthew Henry: Gabriel carries his message as gladly to Nazareth in Galilee as to the temple in Jerusalem. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_001.cfm

**v. 27**
- **Traditional Protestant reading:**
  - Mary had never had sexual relations, and since John's conception was a miracle, we should expect the Messiah's to be even more remarkable. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/
  - MacArthur says Luke calls her a virgin twice. The betrothal was a legal bond (*kiddushin*) that usually lasted a year. https://www.gty.org/blogs/print/B141203/mary-an-angelic-announcement
  - Coffman: in every respect except living together, the betrothal was the marriage, and unfaithfulness during it was a capital offence. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-27.html
- **Catholic reading:** Catholic.com uses this verse with v. 34 to argue for Mary's lifelong virginity. Why would she ask how she could conceive if she were in a normal, soon-to-be-consummated marriage with Joseph? It disputes James White's answer that she was "only engaged". https://www.catholic.com/audio/scw/biblical-evidence-for-marys-perpetual-virginity-2
